newsitem.title: UK: "Dark forces" of British politics come into open.
newsitem.headline: "Dark forces" of British politics come into open.

text.p: The "people who live in the dark" in British political life are being forced into the open.
The "spin doctors" -- aides whose job is to ensure favourable media treatment for their political bosses -- have themselves become targets of the media spotlight.
Far from revelling in the attention, the hunters of the press room have turned edgy now they have become the hunted.

The BBC chose the first full day of the opposition Labour party's annual conference to broadcast a 40-minute analysis of "spin doctors," naming key backroom aides in a breach of the unwritten rules governing British political reporting.
The programme listed examples of when aides from both the ruling Conservative and the opposition Labour party had sought to influence news coverage in their favour.
"They push and push and push and push," said Michael Brunson, political editor of ITN, which provides the flagship news programmes for Britain's independent television companies.
Alastair Campbell, press officer to Labour leader Tony Blair and featured prominently in the Panorama programme, denied all comment on the broadcast on Monday night.

But last week he lashed out at the BBC decision to screen its documentary during the Labour conference, the last before the next general election, calling the public broadcaster arrogant, overstaffed and politically biased.
Campbell's arguments contain more than a touch of irony.

During last year's Labour conference, Campbell stirred up a hornet's nest when he urged the BBC to lead its main evening news programmes with Blair's speech rather than the O.J. Simpson trial verdict just breaking in the United States. The BBC did make Blair the top item, unlike ITN which led on O.J. Simpson.
But the BBC said it decided on editorial grounds, not under pressure. Its director general John Birt also attacked Campbell for what he called a "crass and inappropriate" message.

But whatever the arguments, the programme made clear both parties are unwilling to leave anything to chance as time ticks away to an election which will either end 17 years of Conservative rule or return them for a record fifth term.
Some politicians are growing concerned about the influence of the unaccountable and shadowy backroom figures.
Senior Labour party member Clare Short lashed out recently in an article in the left-of-centre magazine New Statesman at what she called "people who live in the dark".
Short's remarks were widely interpreted as referring to Campbell and Labour MP Peter Mandelson, a close friend of Blair and widely regarded as a master of media manipulation.
Seizing on this, the Conservatives turned Short's comments into the inspiration for a poster campaign depicting Blair as having demon eyes staring out of the dark.
But commentators say the Conservative attacks on Labour's spin doctors has been fuelled at least in part by a string of ruling party losses in the propaganda battle.
The Conservative party's most serious reversal was when its communications director Hugh Colver resigned last year saying "a political propagandist was needed and that is not my style".
Since then the party has also adopted a tough approach.

Earlier this year, Conservative party chairman Brian Mawhinney erupted in anger in an interview on the BBC's morning radio news programme when it was suggested that Prime Minister John Major's position was under threat.
But the signs are the media is not taking it lying down.

The BBC has announced it has been logging any intimidatory pressure from politicians and their aides, proving it is ready to fight back with something feared by those who seek headlines for their political masters -- publicity.
